prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock and its development to uncertainties at the 10^-18 level, opening new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B043) first and optical lattice clocks (B002) second. Having read all eight ballots, I now put B002 first. It is the only shortlisted candidate that six members, including me, placed in their top five. Kroll and Lindroth ranked it first, I ranked it second, Olsson third, and Eriksson and Johansson fifth. The case is the one I value as an experimentalist. The magic-wavelength idea is original and cleanly attributed, with Katori proposing and first demonstrating it and Ye taking it to record accuracy and stability. The headline numbers are quantitative and have been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories. The science reaches beyond metrology to relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-sector searches, and the redefinition of the second is under active discussion. A two-laureate prize is natural here, and no statutory limit forces us to leave out someone essential.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that optical clocks are a measurement technology, and one could argue the field is already well rewarded by the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for quantum control of single ions, so the novelty margin is narrower than the precision figures suggest. Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Wineland-group ion clocks have real claims to credit that a Katori-Ye prize would pass over. There is also a timing argument for waiting: the redefinition of the second has not happened, and a prize that follows it would be easier to justify. I do not find the timing point decisive, because the performance is established and independently verified.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery (B053) first, because the 2013 prize recognised only the theory and the experimental discovery is overdue, and he ranks IceCube sixth because source populations are still not understood.
responses.response: I agree the Higgs discovery is scientifically as important as anything on the list. My reservation is attribution. Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee are founding leaders, but the discovery was made by two collaborations of thousands in 2012, and a prize to founders rather than to the people who delivered the 2012 analyses is exposed to fair challenge. Kroll and Lindroth also placed it only third and fourth, so it has less breadth than clocks. I take your IceCube point seriously and have lowered IceCube accordingly. The diffuse flux is secure, but the source picture is incomplete and Spiering's credit relative to other founders is harder to defend than I argued. I would keep B053 as a live alternative but not as the lead.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first and trapped-ion quantum computing and simulation (B033) second, citing Cirac and Zoller as theoretical originators and Blatt as the experimental realiser.
responses.response: I share your first choice and your view that the attribution to Katori and Ye is clean. I am more cautious than you about B033. The 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche already covers the trapped-ion control that the Cirac-Zoller programme builds on, and Johansson makes the same point on overlap. Blatt's group realised the gates, but the credit is split among several ion-trap laboratories, including NIST, so the three-name allocation is contestable. I would want that disentangled before ranking B033 above lattice clocks.

responses.point: Lindroth places lattice clocks first and stresses maturity: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB and NIST have all reproduced and surpassed the original performance.
responses.response: That is the argument that moved me, and I accept it over my own enthusiasm for a detector story. As someone who builds instruments, I treat independent reproduction across many national laboratories as a stronger signal than a single flagship facility. Where I would qualify your ballot is on adding quantum-simulation or squeezed-light candidates alongside clocks. Squeezed light (B019) has the weakest opening support on the list, a diffuse credit among Caves, Kimble, Schnabel and Mavalvala, and a gravitational-wave application that is credited elsewhere.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B017) first and magic-angle graphene (B038) second, and ranks lattice clocks only fifth.
responses.response: I disagree on circuit QED as a lead. The four credited names (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin) cannot be reduced to three without leaving out an originator of the 2004 proposal, and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes the timing sensitive, as Olsson and Lindroth both note. On magic-angle graphene I agree it is a clean theory-plus-experiment trio, but you yourself say the field is only about eight years old and the superconducting mechanism is debated. That maturity concern is exactly what makes me keep it as an alternative rather than the lead.

uncertainties: Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes leave enough room for a further precision-metrology prize in atomic physics.
Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second before awarding lattice clocks.
Whether Lemonde, Ludlow or the ion-clock groups have credit that makes a two-person Katori-Ye allocation unfair.
How much weight to give magic-angle graphene (B038), which has the broadest top-three support among the condensed-matter candidates, given the open question about the superconducting mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for lattice clocks (B002) or the alternatives I name. My documented connections are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, and my field is astroparticle physics, so IceCube is scientifically close to my own work and I have disclosed that in treating it as an alternative. I have no recorded tie to the candidates for B002, B043 or B038.
